opus-5.5.text:
I think a lot of it comes down to the fact that the people who know robotics best have also been burned the most. If you've spent twenty years in this field, you've watched wave after wave of hype come and go. You've seen the demos that looked incredible on stage and then fell apart the moment they hit a real warehouse or a real home. So there's a kind of earned skepticism, and honestly, for a long time that skepticism was correct.

But I think what's different now is that the bottleneck has shifted. For decades, the hard problem wasn't the hardware so much as the intelligence. You could build a capable arm or a mobile base, but getting it to handle the messiness of the real world meant hand-engineering every behavior, every edge case. That doesn't scale. What we're seeing now with foundation models, large-scale data collection, simulation, and learning from demonstration is that the software side is starting to generalize in ways it never did before. And when the intelligence starts to generalize, the economics change very quickly.

Experts tend to think linearly because their experience has been linear: slow, incremental progress, one painful deployment at a time. But a lot of these underlying curves, compute, data, model capability, the cost of actuators and sensors, are compounding at the same time. When several exponentials overlap, things go from "not quite working" to "good enough to deploy" faster than intuition suggests.

There's also a bit of a definitional issue. Roboticists often hold out for the general-purpose robot that can do anything a human can. But robots don't need to be perfect to get out into the world. They need to be useful and cost-effective for a specific job, in a specific environment, with some human oversight. That bar is much lower, and we're already crossing it in logistics, manufacturing, agriculture, and inspection. Once robots are deployed, they generate more data, which makes them better, which justifies more deployment. That flywheel is what I think a lot of people are underestimating.

So it's not that the experts are wrong about how hard the problems are. They're right about that. It's that they may be underestimating how fast the tools for solving those problems are improving, and how little perfection you actually need to start creating real value.

r001.rationale: The response cites experts’ past exposure to hype and failed deployments as grounds for skepticism, but does not attribute their underestimation to project fatigue.

r002.rationale: It mentions no plan to produce 10,000 robots this year and does not contrast such production with a prediction of deployment being 10 to 15 years away.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think it's because experts, almost by definition, are the people who know exactly how hard the problem is. If you've spent twenty years trying to get a hand to pick up a crumpled piece of paper without dropping it, you've got a very vivid sense of every failure mode. You've seen the demo that looked perfect and then fell apart the moment the lighting changed. So you calibrate on the hard parts, and you assume the world is going to wait for those hard parts to be solved before robots show up anywhere.

But that's not how deployment actually works. Robots don't need to solve the general problem to get out into the world. They need to solve a narrow enough problem that someone is willing to pay for it, and then the environment gets reshaped around them. Warehouses are a perfect example. Nobody waited for a robot that could navigate a cluttered human space. They put down floor markers, standardized the totes, built the shelves to the robot's spec. The robot didn't get smarter, the building got dumber in exactly the right way. And the experts, looking at it from the lab, see a system that's still brittle in a hundred ways and think, "that's not real autonomy." Meanwhile there are hundreds of thousands of them running shifts.

The other piece is that a lot of what's changing right now isn't coming from robotics labs at all. The learning stack, the perception models, the ability to go from a handful of demonstrations to a policy that generalizes a bit, that's coming from the broader machine learning world and it's moving at a pace roboticists aren't used to. For most of the field's history, progress came from mechanical engineering and control theory, where you earned every inch. When your intuition is built on that, it's hard to internalize that a model trained on video data might hand you a capability in six months that you'd have budgeted a decade for.

And honestly, there's a little bit of a defensive reflex in there too. If you've built a career on the difficulty of a problem, and someone shows up saying it's about to get a lot easier, your first instinct is to list all the reasons they're wrong. Usually they are partly wrong. But "partly wrong" is often enough to ship something.

r001.rationale: The response attributes underestimation to experts’ familiarity with technical difficulty, lab-based assumptions, and a defensive reflex; it does not mention project fatigue.

r002.rationale: It gives warehouse robots as an example of deployment, but does not mention the speaker’s plan to produce 10,000 robots this year or predictions of a 10-to-15-year wait.

astra-6.text:
I think robotics experts understand how hard robotics is, and that can make them underestimate how quickly it can become useful. They see all the edge cases—the things a robot still can’t do reliably. But a customer doesn’t necessarily need a robot that can do everything. They need it to do one valuable job consistently.

If you can put a robot into a reasonably controlled environment and have it take a repetitive task off someone’s plate, there’s a business case today. You don’t have to solve every problem in robotics before you start deploying. And once you deploy, you learn what actually matters to the customer, which makes the next version better. I think that cycle is going to move faster than people expect.

r001.rationale: The response points to experts focusing on robotics’ edge cases, but does not attribute their underestimation to project fatigue.

r002.rationale: It mentions deployment and business cases today, but does not cite a plan to produce 10,000 robots this year or challenge a 10-to-15-year prediction.

sol-6.1.text:
I think when you work in robotics every day, you’re very aware of everything that doesn’t work. You see the edge cases, the failures, and all the things you still need to solve. And it’s easy to turn that into a belief that robots are a long way from being useful.

But a customer doesn’t need a robot that can do everything. They need a robot that can solve a particular problem reliably and at a price that makes sense. If you can do that, there’s a reason to deploy it today. Then you learn from that deployment and improve.

So I think the gap is between looking at how far we are from a general-purpose robot and looking at how many useful jobs robots can already start doing. Those are very different ways of measuring progress.

r001.rationale: The response says experts focus on failures and unsolved problems, but does not attribute their underestimation to project fatigue.

r002.rationale: It gives no production plan or figure of 10,000 robots this year and does not challenge a 10-to-15-year deployment prediction.
